title: A Choir for the Well
premise: Paloma Dunmore, a nonbinary urban documentarian, inherits Dunmore House from a grandmother they never met and discovers the estate sits atop a network of tunnels absent from every survey—tunnels that hum when sung to. The house's founders built a choir of the living and the dead to keep something patient and hungry asleep beneath the hill, and every generation has owed it voices. When mirrors begin lagging reality by one second, Paloma realizes their documentation—their prayer—has been read aloud by something below, marking them as the final voice. To save the town and the person they've come to love, they must complete the interrupted ritual: not by sacrificing themselves as duty demands, but by teaching the thing below its own name, turning power into recognition. The house falls silent at last—but Paloma leaves one recording behind, for whoever inherits next.
about_author: Silas Fairweather is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing sealed estates in New England before turning to fiction. They write horror about paperwork, inheritance, and the terrible intimacy of old houses.

chapters.title: The Deed and the Dead
chapters.summary: Paloma arrives at Dunmore House with recording equipment and a lawyer's letter, POV theirs throughout. Exploring the ground floor, they find grandmother Edith's journals full of musical notation that maps onto floorplans. Emotional beat: wary curiosity curdling into unease when every door in the east wing is locked from the inside.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. They begin their methodical survey, photographing and logging, and notice their own voice echoes a half-beat wrong in the stairwell. A neighbor, Wren Halloway, warns them off the cellar with genuine fear. Beat: Paloma's compulsive need to record established as both armor and vulnerability.

chapters.title: Tunnels Not on Any Survey
chapters.summary: Paloma breaks into the cellar and finds a bricked archway breathing warm air. Beyond it, hand-cut tunnels run beneath the town, walls scored with hymn lyrics in generations of handwriting. Beat: awe giving way to dread as they realize the tunnels predate the house above them.

chapters.title: The Founders' Score
chapters.summary: Paloma deciphers Edith's journals: in 1847, seven founders bound something beneath the hill using a choral ritual requiring living voices each generation. The last performance was 1974—and incomplete. Beat: intellectual thrill shadowed by the realization that incompleteness has consequences still accruing.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: The mirrors begin reflecting rooms one second behind. Paloma films them obsessively; in the lag, figures appear that aren't in the room—a congregation of faces, singing silently. Beat: terror fused with fascination; Paloma can't stop watching.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: Wren Halloway's POV. She tends the town's small church and knows more than she admits: her family were the ritual's organists. She and Paloma grow close over shared records and shared insomnia. Beat: tenderness blooming in a haunted place; first real intimacy.

chapters.title: What the House Owes
chapters.summary: Paloma learns the inheritance was never accidental—Edith chose them precisely because they're unaffiliated, unbaptized, undocumented by any church. A 'clean voice.' Beat: betrayal and anger; love against duty takes shape as Paloma refuses the role assigned to them.

chapters.title: The Congregation Below
chapters.summary: Paloma descends again with Wren and finds the founders' descendants—townsfolk who've been singing in shifts for decades, gray-faced and tireless. Their choirmaster, Mr. Voss, welcomes Paloma like a returning soloist. Beat: horror of willing complicity; the town itself is complicit.

chapters.title: Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Voss insists Paloma rehearse the final movement, claiming the thing below grows restless without completion—sinkholes, sleepwalking children, livestock found facing downhill. Paloma sings once and the tunnels answer in harmony. Beat: seduction of belonging; the music is beautiful, which is worse.

chapters.title: Edith's Last Recording
chapters.summary: Paloma restores a reel-to-reel tape from 1974: Edith's voice mid-ritual, then a scream, then silence, then Edith whispering 'don't finish it—rename it.' Beat: grief for the grandmother they never knew, and the first hint of an alternative to sacrifice.

chapters.title: The Lag Widens
chapters.summary: Mirrors now lag five seconds; reflections act independently, mouthing warnings. Paloma realizes the reflected room is the tunnel-world bleeding through. Wren's church organ plays itself at night. Beat: escalating dread; reality's seams showing.

chapters.title: Voss's Sermon
chapters.summary: Voss gathers the town, revealing the truth openly: the founders' bargain bought prosperity, and prosperity must be repaid in voices. He frames Paloma's refusal as selfishness. Beat: power's corruption made explicit; the crowd's frightened agreement is the true horror.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Wren offers to take Paloma's place in the ritual, insisting her family's debt makes it hers. Paloma refuses to let her. First kiss, in the mirror-lagged hallway where their reflections are already holding hands. Beat: fierce tenderness; stakes become personal.

chapters.title: The Name Beneath
chapters.summary: Cross-referencing Edith's tapes and tunnel inscriptions, Paloma reconstructs what the founders buried: not a demon but a chorus itself—the drowned quarry singers of 1846, whose mass death the founders caused and then exploited. Beat: moral vertigo; the monster was made, and named, by men.

chapters.title: Intermission
chapters.summary: A false calm: the lag stops, mirrors clear, tunnels go quiet. Voss declares victory; the town relaxes. Paloma alone suspects the silence is listening. Beat: dread of the pause before catastrophe; isolation deepens.

chapters.title: The Unfinished Movement
chapters.summary: The thing below finishes the 1974 ritual itself, badly, using stolen voices—including Edith's recorded ones. The house begins folding inward; reflections now precede actions. Beat: chaos and guilt; Paloma's archive became ammunition.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Paloma and Wren descend with every recording Paloma owns, past the exhausted congregation, toward the source of the humming. Voss follows, intending to force the original ending. Beat: resolve hardened into purpose; no more documenting—intervening.

chapters.title: The Choir for the Well
chapters.summary: Climax part one: in the flooded quarry chamber, Voss attempts the sacrificial rite on Paloma. Wren shatters his control by playing the founders' score backwards on a portable player, unraveling his authority. Beat: desperate action; duty weaponized against its enforcer.

chapters.title: Renaming
chapters.summary: Climax part two: instead of completing the ritual, Paloma sings the drowned singers their own names—one hundred and twelve of them, recovered from quarry ledgers—giving the entity recognition instead of obedience. The hunger becomes mourning; the well fills with sound, then stillness. Beat: catharsis through witness; love expressed as attention.

chapters.title: Aftermath in One Second
chapters.summary: The mirrors reflect in perfect time. The congregation wakes, aged and free; Voss, hollowed, walks into the sealed tunnels voluntarily. The town must live with what it did. Beat: somber relief; corruption exposed but not erased.

chapters.title: What We Keep
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Paloma and Wren restore the house together, deciding what to preserve and what to bury. Paloma archives everything except one tape. Beat: quiet healing; documentation transformed from prayer to memory.

chapters.title: For Whoever Inherits Next
chapters.summary: Final chapter, epistolary: Paloma seals one recording—of the renamed singers, singing freely—in the cellar wall with instructions: listen, don't obey. Driving away, Paloma checks the rearview mirror; the reflection waves back, kindly, in time. Beat: bittersweet closure with an open door.
